name: Web reference architectures: SUMO-Web3D, alexose/traffic-visualizer, FOSS4G 2025/2026 Korean web traffic simulation platform
type: simulator (three reference web architectures: server-side engine streaming to browser; engine in browser as Rust/WASM; microservice platform with scenario editor)
maintainer: SUMO-Web3D: Sidewalk Labs (github.com/sidewalklabs/sumo-web3d; not eclipse-sumo/sumo-web3d, which does not exist). traffic-visualizer: individual developer Alex Ose (github.com/alexose). FOSS4G platform: Hansang Kim and Sungjo Min (FOSS4G 2025 talk); Cheun-gill Park (Gaia3D, Head of DT Department) and Kim Deokhyeon (FOSS4G 2026 talk); funded by Korean IITP grant RS-2024-00459703
first_release: SUMO-Web3D: repository created 2017-12-21, PyPI 1.0.0 on 2018-02-22. traffic-visualizer: commits from January 2026, repository created 2026-02-08. FOSS4G platform: presented 2025-11-20 (FOSS4G 2025) and 2026-09-01 (FOSS4G 2026, described as the project's third year)
last_activity: SUMO-Web3D: last code commit 2018-11-15, PyPI 1.0.1 on 2018-06-14, repository archived (read-only). traffic-visualizer: last commit 2026-02-08 ('Adding stuff'), 12 commits total, 3 stars. FOSS4G platform: FOSS4G 2026 talk 2026-09-01; no public repository found
licence: SUMO-Web3D: EPL-2.0. traffic-visualizer: no licence file (GitHub reports none), so default copyright applies and reuse needs the author's permission. FOSS4G platform: [uncertain] no software licence stated; only the 2026 talk materials are CC BY 4.0
language: SUMO-Web3D: Python 3 server (aiohttp, websockets, lxml, xmltodict) + TypeScript/React/three.js client. traffic-visualizer: Python data pipeline, Rust simulation compiled to WASM with wasm-bindgen, TypeScript WebGL2 renderer. FOSS4G platform: CesiumJS (3D), OpenLayers (2D WebGL), PostGIS/PostgreSQL; engine language not disclosed
code_availability: SUMO-Web3D: source at https://github.com/sidewalklabs/sumo-web3d and pip package sumo-web3d. traffic-visualizer: source at https://github.com/alexose/traffic-visualizer (no licence). FOSS4G platform: talk abstracts and a workflow PDF only; no repository found under the Gaia3D GitHub organisation (checked: no traffic-related repository) - code availability unconfirmed
maintenance_health: SUMO-Web3D: dead since 2018 and archived; pinned to SUMO 0.31-era tooling, and the README warns Mac users must build SUMO themselves. traffic-visualizer: a one-month personal prototype, single author, no releases, no licence. FOSS4G platform: an active government-funded R&D project (2025 to 2026) but closed or unpublished code.
scale: SUMO-Web3D: inherits SUMO (microscopic). traffic-visualizer: agent-based with an IDM module plus per-edge congested-speed and maximum-exit-rate state, so it looks like a micro/meso hybrid [uncertain]. FOSS4G platform: not disclosed; designed to integrate 'external traffic modeling engines'
car_following: SUMO-Web3D: whatever SUMO is configured with (default Krauss); it is only a visualiser. traffic-visualizer: Intelligent Driver Model (simulation/src/idm.rs). FOSS4G platform: not disclosed
lane_model: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO lanes, rendered in 3D. traffic-visualizer: commit history adds 'Lanes' and 'Parking'; details undocumented [uncertain]. FOSS4G platform: not disclosed
lateral_model_type: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO's (none by default, sublane if configured). traffic-visualizer: [uncertain] none found. FOSS4G platform: not disclosed
junction_model: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO's junction model, with junction shapes from the .net.xml reformatted by the Python server for the client. traffic-visualizer: [uncertain] undocumented; network built by the Python pipeline from OSM. FOSS4G platform: not disclosed
signal_control_modes: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO signals, read-only in the viewer. Others: not documented
flyover_support: SUMO-Web3D renders elevated roads in 3D (README screenshot 'elevated highway'). FOSS4G 2026 platform claims an interface to control 'overpasses and underpasses' in the scenario editor, with CesiumJS terrain. traffic-visualizer: [uncertain] no evidence
grade_separation_handling: SUMO-Web3D draws SUMO's z coordinates; it does no import checking. FOSS4G 2026 lists overpass/underpass editing as a new UX feature but gives no algorithm. traffic-visualizer: not documented
vehicle_types: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO vehicle and person types (cars, buses, pedestrians shown). traffic-visualizer: trip types coloured by purpose ('Trip types + color' commit). FOSS4G: not disclosed
gridlock_policy: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO's (teleport by default). Others: not documented
mixed_traffic_support: None of the three addresses Indian mixed traffic; SUMO-Web3D could show SUMO sublane runs.
non_lane_behaviour: Not addressed by any of the three (SUMO-Web3D only passes through whatever SUMO computes).
seepage_filtering_support: Not addressed by any of the three.
per_class_parameters: None published by any of the three.
indian_calibration_evidence: None; the targets are Bologna/Toronto demo scenarios (SUMO-Web3D), Portland, Oregon (traffic-visualizer) and Seoul/Daejeon (FOSS4G).
calibration_dataset_used: traffic-visualizer: OSM, Oregon Metro RLIS parcels, US Census ACS, LEHD LODES commute flows (synthetic population). FOSS4G: Seoul and Daejeon transport network and station data (GeoJSON/PostGIS). SUMO-Web3D: SUMO example scenarios.
calibration_method: [uncertain] None documented for any of the three.
network_import: SUMO-Web3D: reads SUMO .net.xml and poly files (built beforehand with netconvert/osmWebWizard), and the server reformats them for three.js. traffic-visualizer: an offline Python pipeline fetches OSM plus local datasets and emits binary files the WASM engine loads (load_network, load_routes, load_agents, load_parking, load_corridors). FOSS4G platform: GeoJSON and PostGIS network and station data, with 2026 adding import/export for external simulation engines and GIS formats.
demand_input_formats: SUMO-Web3D: SUMO route files via .sumocfg (with --sumo-args such as --scale 10). traffic-visualizer: synthetic agents from census and LEHD flows, precomputed by the pipeline. FOSS4G: 'demand conditions' configured in the scenario editor (format not disclosed).
data_access: traffic-visualizer data are US public datasets fetched by 'make data'. Others: N/A.
runs_in_browser_or_server: SUMO-Web3D: engine on the server (SUMO subprocess + Python TraCI bridge), rendering in the browser. traffic-visualizer: engine and rendering both in the browser (Rust->WASM + WebGL2), with only static files served. FOSS4G platform: server-side microservices with a browser client (OpenLayers 2D editing, CesiumJS 3D playback).
wasm_or_streaming_feasibility: SUMO-Web3D demonstrates streaming: the server keeps a list of vehicles and people and sends 'frame-by-frame diffs' over a WebSocket to a three.js client. traffic-visualizer demonstrates WASM: a Simulation object exposing tick(dt), get_visible_agents(bbox) -> Vec<f32> (flat float buffer for the GPU), get_stats and get_congestion_stats. FOSS4G: microservices so each function scales independently, with a shared state-management layer between Cesium and OpenLayers.
api: SUMO-Web3D: TraCI between server and SUMO; WebSocket JSON diffs to the client; scenarios registered in scenarios.json. traffic-visualizer: wasm-bindgen JS class (new, load_*, tick, get_visible_agents, get_stats). FOSS4G: not published.
performance: [uncertain] None of the three publishes vehicle counts or real-time factors. For SUMO-Web3D, the SUMO TraCI docs give a reference cost: the Bologna scenario (9,000 vehicles, 5,000 steps) takes about 8 s without TraCI, 42 s with subscriptions and 90 s with naive per-vehicle Python queries, so per-step TraCI extraction dominates. The FOSS4G 2026 talk claims large networks render 'without latency' but gives no numbers.
gpu_requirement: No CUDA. All three need WebGL (WebGL2 for traffic-visualizer) in the client browser.
multi_tenancy_model: SUMO-Web3D: one SUMO subprocess per server process and a single shared simulation, so every viewer sees the same run; per-user scenarios would need one process per session. traffic-visualizer: fully client-side, so each user runs their own simulation at zero server cost. FOSS4G: microservices (details not disclosed).
build_complexity: SUMO-Web3D: 'pip install sumo-web3d' plus a system SUMO install and SUMO_HOME; stale (2018) dependencies, so expect breakage with current SUMO and Python. traffic-visualizer: Python 3.10+, Rust + wasm-pack, Node 18+, with 'make data', 'make wasm' and 'make dev'. FOSS4G: not available.
scenario_editability: SUMO-Web3D: none (view only; scenario chosen from a dropdown). traffic-visualizer: playback speed and agent inspection; no network editing. FOSS4G platform: the only one with a scenario editor (modify road network and route structure, configure demand, Edit -> Simulate -> Visualize -> Analyze workflow, side-by-side scenario comparison, time filter, route-change analyser; 2026 adds overpass/underpass control and dashboard reports).
output_metrics_supported: SUMO-Web3D: visual only. traffic-visualizer: aggregate stats and per-zone congestion. FOSS4G: route-change analysis, scenario comparison, trip lines and OD matrices (companion 2025 visualisation talk), and policy dashboards (2026).
emissions_support: None in the three web layers themselves (SUMO's own emission models would be available behind SUMO-Web3D).
reuse_mode: Inspiration only for all three. SUMO-Web3D: copy the pattern (TraCI subscription -> diff -> WebSocket -> three.js), not the archived code. traffic-visualizer: copy the pattern (WASM tick + flat Float32 buffer for the visible bounding box -> WebGL2 instanced draw); the code cannot be legally reused without a licence. FOSS4G: copy the product workflow (Edit -> Simulate -> Visualize -> Compare); there is no code to reuse.
effort_within_72_hours: SUMO-Web3D pattern: about 4-8 hours for a minimal FastAPI/aiohttp + libsumo or TraCI loop pushing JSON or binary diffs over a WebSocket to deck.gl/MapLibre; reviving the archived repo itself is likely slower than rewriting [uncertain]. traffic-visualizer pattern: about 4-6 hours to set up the wasm-pack + WebGL/deck.gl skeleton, but the engine itself must still be written. FOSS4G workflow: the scenario editor is the expensive part; within 72 hours cut it to editing a few parameters (lane count/width, signal timings, demand multipliers) on a fixed network rather than free-form road drawing.
licence_constraint: SUMO-Web3D EPL-2.0: weak copyleft at file level; modified EPL files must be released as source, but separate files of our own can use any licence. traffic-visualizer: no licence, so the code cannot legally be copied; only ideas can be reused. FOSS4G: no code; talk materials CC BY 4.0 (attribution).
known_limitations: SUMO-Web3D: archived, no editing, a single shared simulation, needs a native SUMO install, dependencies frozen at 2018 versions. traffic-visualizer: 12-commit prototype, US-specific data pipeline, no licence, no documentation of the model, no editing. FOSS4G platform: code not public, no performance numbers, engine unnamed; the Korean context (lane-based) does not transfer to Indian mixed traffic.
documented_failures: [uncertain] No post-mortems published. Inferred risk: SUMO-Web3D was abandoned after Sidewalk Labs' 2018 work and has not tracked SUMO releases, the usual fate of a visualiser tightly coupled to a fast-moving engine's file formats.
validation_approach: Visual demonstration only (screenshots, demo scenarios; conference talks). No quantitative validation in any of the three.
takeaway_for_our_build: Pick one of two proven shapes and do not mix them: (a) server engine -> WebSocket diffs (SUMO-Web3D shape), or (b) WASM engine in the browser -> flat Float32 buffers -> WebGL instanced rendering (traffic-visualizer shape). In both, send only positions of agents inside the current viewport, as compact typed arrays rather than per-vehicle JSON, because TraCI per-vehicle polling alone is about 11x slower than plain SUMO. Borrow the FOSS4G product loop (Edit -> Simulate -> Visualize -> Compare two scenarios side by side), since comparing scenarios is what planners value. Make overpass/underpass editing an explicit editor feature, as the Korean team had to add in year three. Do not depend on any of these codebases: one is archived, one is unlicensed and one is unpublished.
